title: Why keep saints' days
hookLine: remembering holy people on their day, as families remember birthdays

cards: A paper calendar on a kitchen wall, birthdays circled in pen: Grandma, a cousin, the neighbor's twins. Nobody needs a reason to keep them. People are remembered on their day because they belong to someone.
Now a different calendar, the kind churches keep. Square after square, a name: Agnes, Benedict, Mary Magdalene, Nicholas. And here's the twist.

By old custom, the date beside a saint's name is often not the day they were born. It's the day they died. A new block begins, a year of feasts and saints' days, with one question: why keep them at all?

teach.b: Start with the word saint. In Paul's letters it doesn't mean a few well-known holy people. He writes "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi": the whole congregation, whoever they were.
Saints, in that letter, are simply God's people. Then Christians began remembering particular ones. An early account tells of Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, put to death for his faith.

Afterward his church wrote that they gathered his bones and laid them to rest, and meant to meet there with joy and keep the day of his martyrdom as a birthday: to remember those who had finished the race, and to train those still running.
A birthday into heaven. Tradition gave it a Latin name, dies natalis.

teach.h: REMEMBER THEM, AND FOLLOW THEIR FAITH.
teach.b: Some find the reason in Hebrews: "Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow". Remember, and follow.
And a psalm says: "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints."
Churches keep these days differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep full calendars, celebrate the saints at the liturgy, and ask them to pray for the living, the way you'd ask a friend.
Anglicans and Lutherans keep calendars of saints and commemorations too, with their own emphases.
Some other Protestant churches keep no saints' days, honoring faithful people in sermons and stories and directing every prayer to God alone. Each reads the same Hebrews line.
This block walks through the year's feasts and those names, one day at a time.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches mark saints' days in their calendars, with readings, prayers and sometimes feasts; some other Protestant churches honor faithful Christians of the past in sermons and stories without a calendar of saints.

games.why: the Martyrdom of Polycarp says they laid his bones to rest and planned to meet there with joy, keeping the day of his martyrdom as a birthday.

practice: Stay close to home: someone who passed something good on to you, a grandparent who said grace, a teacher, a neighbor, someone you've lost.
Picture their face, their hands, one good thing they did, and let it be their day for a moment. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them; if you don't, simply remember them with care.

wordCard.voice: Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the church's old name for a saint's day of death, the day their life began in heaven.
